questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks' gestation attends the clinic reporting a severe frontal headache, blurred vision and sudden swelling of her hands. Her blood pressure is higher than at previous visits. Which nursing action is the highest priority?

options.text: Repeat the blood pressure, assess urine for protein, assess fetal wellbeing and arrange urgent medical review.
Reassure her that swelling and headache are common late-pregnancy discomforts and arrange routine follow-up.
Advise rest at home, increased oral fluids and reduced salt intake.
Provide simple analgesia and ask her to return if symptoms persist for 24 hours.

questions.rationale: Severe headache, visual disturbance, sudden swelling and raised blood pressure are danger signs that may indicate a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. Maternal assessment, urine testing, fetal assessment and urgent escalation are required.

questions.stem: During an antenatal assessment, a woman at 28 weeks says her baby has moved much less than usual since the previous evening. She has no pain or bleeding. What is the most appropriate nursing response?

options.text: Explain that fetal movement normally decreases significantly in the third trimester.
Treat reduced fetal movement as significant, complete the appropriate maternal and fetal assessment and arrange prompt review.
Advise her to wait until the next scheduled appointment.
Recommend a sugary drink and discharge her without further assessment.

questions.rationale: Reduced fetal movement may indicate fetal compromise and should not be dismissed. Prompt assessment and escalation according to local policy are required.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman reports urinary frequency and mild fatigue at 18 weeks. Her observations are stable and she has no dysuria, fever or abdominal pain. How should the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: They indicate a urinary tract infection requiring emergency treatment.
They suggest imminent preterm labour.
They are common physiological adaptations of pregnancy, but the nurse should continue routine assessment and education.
They are evidence of gestational hypertension.

questions.rationale: Urinary frequency and fatigue may be expected adaptations in pregnancy. The absence of pain, fever and other warning signs makes emergency pathology less likely, although routine monitoring remains necessary.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing health education for a woman in early pregnancy. Which teaching plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Advise complete avoidance of physical activity and routine supplements unless symptoms develop.
Recommend doubling all usual vitamin doses to support fetal growth.
Focus only on weight gain because other lifestyle factors have little effect.
Discuss balanced nutrition, recommended folate and iron, safe activity, rest, immunisation guidance, avoidance of harmful substances and attendance at scheduled care.

questions.rationale: Antenatal health promotion includes nutrition, recommended supplementation, safe activity, rest, immunisation advice, avoidance of harmful substances and regular care.

questions.stem: At 30 weeks' gestation, a woman reports a sudden gush of clear fluid from the vagina but no contractions. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Arrange prompt assessment because leaking fluid may indicate rupture of membranes.
Advise her to observe the fluid at home for several hours.
Explain that this is normal urinary leakage in pregnancy.
Recommend pelvic floor exercises and routine follow-up.

questions.rationale: Leaking fluid is a pregnancy danger sign and may indicate rupture of membranes, which requires timely assessment for maternal and fetal risk.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman has mild breathlessness when climbing stairs but is comfortable at rest, has normal oxygen saturation and no chest pain. What is the best nursing interpretation?

options.text: Any breathlessness in pregnancy indicates pulmonary embolism.
Mild exertional breathlessness can be a normal adaptation, but sudden, severe or resting breathlessness requires urgent assessment.
The finding confirms anaemia.
The woman should avoid all activity for the remainder of pregnancy.

questions.rationale: Pregnancy alters respiratory physiology, and mild exertional breathlessness can be expected. Sudden, severe or resting symptoms are not normal and require assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing a routine antenatal assessment. Which combination best reflects assessment of both maternal and fetal wellbeing?

options.text: Maternal weight and diet history only.
Fetal heart rate only.
Blood pressure, urine testing, fetal growth, fetal heart activity and the mother's report of fetal movement.
Maternal pulse and temperature only.

questions.rationale: Antenatal care integrates maternal observations and screening with fetal growth, heart activity and movement.

questions.stem: A woman at 24 weeks presents with vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Provide reassurance because minor bleeding is common at this stage.
Ask her to return if bleeding becomes heavier.
Advise bed rest at home without assessment.
Complete a prompt assessment, avoid unnecessary delay and escalate for urgent obstetric review.

questions.rationale: Bleeding with pain is a danger sign and may represent a serious obstetric complication requiring urgent review.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman asks why urine testing is performed during antenatal visits. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: It can help identify protein, glucose or signs of infection that may indicate maternal or pregnancy complications.
It is performed only to confirm pregnancy.
It replaces blood pressure measurement.
It is used primarily to determine fetal sex.

questions.rationale: Urine testing may contribute to detection of hypertensive disorders, diabetes and infection when interpreted with other findings.

questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks has fever, chills and abdominal discomfort. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Treat the fever as a normal pregnancy response.
Assess maternal observations, fetal wellbeing and possible infection, and arrange urgent review.
Advise routine hydration and wait until the next day.
Recommend non-prescription medication without further assessment.

questions.rationale: Fever during pregnancy may indicate infection and can threaten maternal and fetal wellbeing; urgent assessment is appropriate.

questions.stem: A woman with no previous antenatal care presents late in pregnancy. What should the nurse prioritise?

options.text: Criticising the missed appointments to improve future attendance.
Focusing only on the expected date of birth.
A respectful comprehensive assessment of maternal history, current health, fetal wellbeing, screening needs and barriers to care.
Delaying assessment until prior records are available.

questions.rationale: Late presentation requires non-judgemental comprehensive assessment and identification of health and access needs.

questions.stem: Which finding most clearly distinguishes a pregnancy danger sign from a common discomfort?

options.text: Mild fatigue after activity.
Occasional urinary frequency.
Mild nausea in early pregnancy.
Severe abdominal pain with vaginal bleeding.

questions.rationale: Severe pain with bleeding is not an expected adaptation and requires urgent evaluation.

questions.stem: A woman reports taking an over-the-counter herbal preparation during pregnancy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask what she is taking, how much and why, and advise review with an appropriate clinician or pharmacist.
Assume it is safe because it is natural.
Tell her to stop all medicines immediately.
Document it only if she develops symptoms.

questions.rationale: Herbal products may have uncertain safety or interactions. A complete medication history and professional review are appropriate.

questions.stem: A nurse identifies that a pregnant woman has difficulty reading written health information. Which education approach is best?

options.text: Provide the same detailed leaflet and ask her to sign it.
Use plain language, demonstration, visual aids and teach-back to confirm understanding.
Ask a family member to explain everything later.
Reduce the amount of information and avoid discussing warning signs.

questions.rationale: Education should be adapted to health literacy while still covering essential safety information.

questions.stem: A woman at 36 weeks reports sudden swelling of her face but no headache. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Reassure her because swelling is always normal near term.
Recommend tighter footwear.
Assess blood pressure, urine and other symptoms, and escalate if findings are concerning.
Advise increased salt intake.

questions.rationale: Sudden facial swelling can be associated with hypertensive disease and warrants assessment.

questions.stem: A woman asks why regular antenatal visits are important when she feels well. Which answer is best?

options.text: They are mainly for completing administrative forms.
They are only necessary for first pregnancies.
They are optional if fetal movement is present.
They help monitor maternal and fetal wellbeing and identify complications before symptoms become severe.

questions.rationale: Regular care supports prevention, screening and early identification of maternal and fetal concerns.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman becomes dizzy and pale while lying flat during an assessment. Which immediate action is most appropriate?

options.text: Reposition her laterally, reassess observations and evaluate her response.
Keep her supine and obtain a full history.
Ask her to stand and walk.
Provide food before reassessment.

questions.rationale: Lateral positioning may reduce compression of major vessels and improve venous return; reassessment is required.

questions.stem: A woman presents with persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down and signs of dehydration. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure her that all vomiting is normal in pregnancy.
Assess hydration, observations and severity and arrange clinical review.
Recommend fasting until symptoms stop.
Advise her to return in one week.

questions.rationale: Persistent vomiting with dehydration is not a simple discomfort and may require treatment.

questions.stem: Which antenatal finding requires the most urgent escalation?

options.text: Mild backache at the end of the day.
Occasional heartburn.
Reduced fetal movement with maternal concern.
Mild ankle swelling after prolonged standing.

questions.rationale: Reduced fetal movement can indicate fetal compromise and requires prompt assessment.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe antenatal nursing care?

options.text: The nurse completes all scheduled forms.
The woman is given general advice only.
All pregnancy symptoms are treated as normal unless bleeding occurs.
Expected changes are explained, maternal and fetal wellbeing are assessed, danger signs are recognised and concerns are escalated early.

questions.rationale: Safe antenatal care combines education, comprehensive assessment and early escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A woman in labour has recurrent fetal heart rate decelerations after contractions. Oxytocin is infusing. What is the nurse's best immediate response?

options.text: Reposition the woman, stop oxytocin according to policy, increase assessment, call for urgent review and prepare for further intervention.
Continue the infusion and observe for another hour.
Encourage pushing regardless of labour stage.
Document the pattern and wait for the next routine review.

questions.rationale: Recurrent post-contraction decelerations may indicate fetal compromise. Immediate supportive actions and urgent escalation are required.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: Which description of the stages of labour is correct?

options.text: The first stage ends with birth and the second ends with placental delivery.
The first stage involves cervical dilatation, the second ends with birth, the third involves placental delivery and the fourth is immediate recovery.
The third stage is cervical dilatation.
The fourth stage begins when contractions first become regular.

questions.rationale: The four stages progress from cervical dilatation to birth, placental delivery and early recovery.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A woman in labour is anxious and says she cannot cope with contractions. Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.text: Tell her that labour pain is unavoidable and she should remain still.
Encourage her family to decide on analgesia.
Assess pain and labour progress, offer position changes, breathing, reassurance and available pain-relief options while supporting informed choice.
Delay comfort measures until cervical dilatation is complete.

questions.rationale: Supportive care includes non-pharmacological and pharmacological options, information and respect for choice.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: Which assessment best reflects care of both mother and fetus during labour?

options.text: Maternal blood pressure only.
Cervical dilatation only.
Contraction frequency only.
Fetal heart rate, contraction pattern, maternal observations, labour progress, pain and emotional wellbeing.

questions.rationale: Labour care requires integrated assessment of the woman, fetus and labour progress.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: The Five Ps of labour include:

options.text: Passenger, passageway, powers, position and psyche.
Pulse, pain, pressure, pelvis and placenta.
Patient, partner, progress, pain and policy.
Position, protein, perfusion, placenta and pulse.

questions.rationale: The Five Ps describe major influences on labour progress.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A woman in labour suddenly reports constant severe abdominal pain between contractions, and fetal heart abnormalities are noted. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Treat this as normal transition and encourage breathing exercises.
Perform urgent assessment and escalate immediately for possible obstetric emergency.
Wait for the next cervical examination.
Offer oral fluids and reassess later.

questions.rationale: Severe continuous pain with fetal compromise may indicate a serious emergency and requires immediate action.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A labouring woman requests to change position frequently. What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Require her to remain supine throughout labour.
Allow movement only during the first stage.
Support movement and position changes if clinically safe and consistent with monitoring requirements.
Explain that movement delays labour.

questions.rationale: Movement and position changes may improve comfort and support labour progress when safe.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: Why should contraction frequency and duration be assessed?

options.text: They are used only to estimate pain.
They replace fetal heart monitoring.
They are irrelevant once membranes rupture.
They help determine labour progress and identify excessive or inadequate uterine activity.

questions.rationale: Contraction characteristics influence labour progress and fetal tolerance.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A woman's membranes rupture and the fluid is greenish. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.text: Assess fetal wellbeing promptly and escalate according to local policy.
Document it as a normal finding.
Encourage ambulation without further assessment.
Delay review until contractions become stronger.

questions.rationale: Abnormal fluid colour may indicate meconium and requires fetal assessment and appropriate escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A woman receiving opioid analgesia in labour becomes very drowsy and has a reduced respiratory rate. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Allow her to sleep and continue routine monitoring.
Assess airway and breathing, seek urgent assistance and follow the medication-response protocol.
Give another dose for comfort.
Encourage oral fluids only.

questions.rationale: Respiratory depression is a serious adverse effect requiring immediate assessment and escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A labouring woman says she does not understand why a proposed intervention is needed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed because labour is time-sensitive.
Ask the family to consent on her behalf.
Provide a clear explanation, check understanding and support informed decision-making unless an immediate emergency prevents delay.
Avoid discussing risks because it may increase anxiety.

questions.rationale: Respectful maternity care includes information, consent and advocacy.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: Which finding during labour is most concerning?

options.text: The woman requests massage.
Contractions become more uncomfortable as labour progresses.
The woman changes position.
The fetal heart pattern becomes persistently abnormal.

questions.rationale: Persistent fetal heart abnormalities may indicate fetal compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A woman is in the third stage of labour. What is the main event occurring?

options.text: Delivery of the placenta.
Cervical dilatation.
Birth of the baby.
Immediate postnatal recovery only.

questions.rationale: The third stage extends from birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A nurse notes that labour progress is slower than expected. Which assessment is most useful?

options.text: Assess pain score only.
Consider the passenger, passageway, powers, position and psyche together.
Increase analgesia automatically.
Assume the woman is not cooperating.

questions.rationale: The Five Ps provide a structured way to consider causes of slow labour.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A woman's fetal heart rate is abnormal, but she asks to continue walking. What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Allow walking because patient choice always overrides safety.
Ask her partner to decide.
Prioritise fetal assessment and explain why monitoring and review are needed before further mobilisation.
Ignore the abnormal finding if she feels well.

questions.rationale: Choice remains important, but urgent safety concerns require explanation, assessment and escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: Which action best supports emotional wellbeing during labour?

options.text: Limit communication to reduce distraction.
Discuss only clinical measurements.
Exclude support people regardless of the woman's wishes.
Provide consistent reassurance, explain progress and involve the woman in decisions.

questions.rationale: Clear communication and participation reduce fear and support coping.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: A woman in labour has very frequent contractions with little rest between them while receiving oxytocin. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recognise possible uterine hyperstimulation, stop or adjust oxytocin according to policy, assess fetal wellbeing and escalate.
Increase the infusion to improve progress.
Wait for the fetal heart rate to become abnormal.
Encourage pushing.

questions.rationale: Excessive contractions can compromise fetal oxygenation and require prompt action.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: During the fourth stage of labour, what is the priority nursing focus?

options.text: Cervical dilatation.
Immediate maternal recovery, bleeding, uterine tone, observations and newborn adaptation.
Fetal position before birth.
Routine discharge planning only.

questions.rationale: The fourth stage focuses on early recovery and detection of complications.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: Which documentation is most important when a fetal heart abnormality occurs?

options.text: Only that the doctor was called.
Only the final outcome.
The pattern, time, maternal and fetal assessments, interventions, escalation and response.
A general statement that the fetus was distressed.

questions.rationale: Detailed objective documentation supports continuity, accountability and review.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe nursing care during labour?

options.text: The labour is completed without analgesia.
The nurse follows one routine for every woman.
Only cervical dilatation is monitored.
The woman receives respectful support while maternal and fetal status are monitored, abnormal patterns are recognised and action is timely.

questions.rationale: Safe labour care combines surveillance, comfort, choice and early escalation.

questions.stem: Two hours after birth, a woman reports dizziness and her pad is rapidly saturating with blood. Her pulse is rising. What should the nurse do FIRST?

options.text: Assess uterine tone and vital signs, call for assistance and initiate the postpartum haemorrhage response.
Reassure her that bleeding is expected after birth.
Ask her to walk to the bathroom.
Wait to weigh the pad before escalating.

questions.rationale: Heavy bleeding with dizziness and tachycardia suggests postpartum haemorrhage and requires immediate assessment and emergency response.

questions.stem: Which assessment is most appropriate during routine postnatal care?

options.text: Blood pressure and temperature only.
Vital signs, uterine tone and position, lochia, bladder, perineum or incision, pain, breasts, mobility and emotional state.
Breastfeeding only.
Wound assessment only.

questions.rationale: Postnatal assessment is systematic and includes physical recovery, feeding and emotional wellbeing.

questions.stem: A postpartum woman's uterus feels boggy and bleeding is increasing. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Encourage sleep.
Delay action until blood pressure falls.
Perform uterine massage where appropriate, call for help and follow the haemorrhage protocol.
Offer oral fluids only.

questions.rationale: A boggy uterus may indicate uterine atony, a common cause of postpartum haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A woman five days after birth has fever, uterine tenderness and foul-smelling lochia. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Normal involution.
Breast engorgement only.
Postnatal blues.
Postnatal infection requiring prompt review.

questions.rationale: Fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia are concerning for infection.

questions.stem: A postnatal woman develops unilateral calf pain and swelling. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Assess and escalate urgently for possible venous thromboembolism.
Massage the calf and encourage walking.
Apply heat and reassess tomorrow.
Reassure her that leg pain is expected.

questions.rationale: Unilateral calf pain and swelling may indicate deep vein thrombosis and should not be massaged or ignored.

questions.stem: A woman suddenly becomes breathless and complains of chest pain three days after birth. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Advise rest and oral fluids.
Treat this as a possible pulmonary embolism and seek emergency assistance.
Explain that breathlessness is common after delivery.
Wait for routine medical review.

questions.rationale: Sudden breathlessness and chest pain in the postnatal period are emergency warning signs.

questions.stem: Which finding is most consistent with normal postnatal emotional adjustment?

options.text: Persistent severe anxiety and inability to care for self or baby.
Thoughts of harming self or the baby.
Brief tearfulness and emotional sensitivity with preserved function and support.
Progressively worsening low mood for several weeks.

questions.rationale: Mild transient emotional change may occur, but persistent or severe symptoms require assessment.

questions.stem: A mother reports persistent low mood, severe anxiety and inability to sleep even when the baby sleeps. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure her this is normal and will pass.
Advise her to avoid discussing the feelings.
Ask the family to manage without professional support.
Complete or arrange timely mental-health assessment and ensure she knows how to access help.

questions.rationale: Persistent, severe or function-limiting symptoms require timely assessment.

questions.stem: Which teaching is most important before postnatal discharge?

options.text: How to recognise heavy bleeding, fever, wound problems, calf pain, breathlessness and severe emotional symptoms.
Only newborn clothing requirements.
Only breastfeeding positions.
Only the date of the next appointment.

questions.rationale: Women and families need clear warning signs and escalation advice.

questions.stem: A woman has increasing wound redness, pain and discharge after caesarean birth. What is the priority?

options.text: Cover the wound and wait several days.
Assess for infection and arrange prompt clinical review.
Encourage vigorous exercise.
Reassure her that discharge is normal.

questions.rationale: These findings may indicate surgical-site infection.

questions.stem: A postnatal woman is unable to void and her uterus is displaced from the midline. What should the nurse consider?

options.text: This is always normal.
The uterus has completed involution.
A full bladder may be affecting uterine position and contraction.
The finding indicates breastfeeding failure.

questions.rationale: Bladder distension can displace the uterus and contribute to poor uterine tone and bleeding.

questions.stem: Why is assessment of lochia important?

options.text: It is used only to estimate hydration.
It replaces uterine assessment.
It is irrelevant after the first hour.
Changes in amount, colour and odour can help identify haemorrhage or infection.

questions.rationale: Lochia is a key indicator of postnatal recovery and complications.

questions.stem: A mother reports painful cracked nipples and the baby is feeding poorly. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Observe a feed, assess attachment and swallowing, and provide practical support.
Tell her to stop breastfeeding permanently.
Advise feeding less often.
Apply any available cream without assessment.

questions.rationale: Poor attachment may contribute to nipple trauma and ineffective feeding.

questions.stem: Which action best supports bonding in the postnatal period?

options.text: Separate mother and baby routinely.
Encourage skin-to-skin contact and responsive interaction when mother and baby are clinically stable.
Discourage family involvement.
Delay contact until discharge.

questions.rationale: Skin-to-skin contact and responsive care support bonding and feeding.

questions.stem: A woman's support person asks for detailed information, but the mother has not consented. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Provide all information because the person is family.
Discuss care outside the room.
Respect the mother's confidentiality and ask whom she wants involved.
Ask another nurse to decide.

questions.rationale: Information sharing should respect consent and confidentiality.

questions.stem: A mother becomes increasingly weak and pale, but visible bleeding appears modest. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume she is tired.
Delay observations.
Encourage ambulation.
Consider concealed or underestimated blood loss, assess urgently and escalate.

questions.rationale: Postpartum haemorrhage may be underestimated; clinical signs must be taken seriously.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests effective postnatal recovery?

options.text: Stable observations, firm uterus, expected lochia, controlled pain, safe mobility and adequate support.
Absence of pain only.
Discharge within 24 hours.
Successful breastfeeding only.

questions.rationale: Recovery should be assessed across multiple physical and psychosocial domains.

questions.stem: A woman reports thoughts of harming herself. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Advise rest and routine follow-up.
Ensure immediate safety, do not leave her alone and arrange urgent mental-health assessment.
Ask her not to discuss the thoughts.
Wait for family confirmation.

questions.rationale: Thoughts of harm require immediate safety measures and urgent assessment.

questions.stem: Which action best supports safe postnatal discharge?

options.text: Provide written instructions only.
Assume family support is available.
Begin planning early, assess physical recovery, emotional wellbeing, feeding, support and understanding of warning signs.
Focus only on the baby's condition.

questions.rationale: Safe discharge depends on maternal recovery, newborn care, support and understanding.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe postnatal nursing care?

options.text: The woman is discharged quickly.
Only bleeding is monitored.
Emotional health is discussed only if the woman asks.
Complications are recognised early, recovery is monitored systematically and education supports safe care at home.

questions.rationale: Comprehensive postnatal nursing includes physical and emotional assessment, feeding support and education.

questions.stem: A newborn is sleepy, feeds poorly and has a low temperature. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Warm the baby, assess breathing and colour, check blood glucose according to policy and escalate for neonatal review.
Assume the baby is simply tired after birth.
Offer water and reassess later.
Delay assessment until the next feed.

questions.rationale: Poor feeding, lethargy and hypothermia may indicate hypoglycaemia, infection or other illness and require prompt assessment.

questions.stem: What are the immediate priorities after birth?

options.text: Bathing, weighing and dressing first.
Airway, breathing, circulation, warmth and observation.
Feeding before breathing assessment.
Routine documentation before contact.

questions.rationale: Immediate newborn care focuses on adaptation and thermoregulation.

questions.stem: Which statement about Apgar scoring is correct?

options.text: It predicts long-term development with certainty.
It replaces clinical examination.
It provides a structured description of adaptation but does not replace ongoing assessment.
A normal score eliminates the need for monitoring.

questions.rationale: Apgar is a useful structured observation, but ongoing assessment remains essential.

questions.stem: A newborn has central cyanosis, grunting and chest retractions. What is the priority?

options.text: Routine skin-to-skin contact without assessment.
Wait for the next scheduled observation.
Feed immediately.
Urgent neonatal assessment and respiratory support according to protocol.

questions.rationale: Central cyanosis and respiratory distress signs are neonatal emergencies.

questions.stem: Why is thermoregulation especially important in newborns?

options.text: They lose heat quickly, and cold stress can increase oxygen and glucose use.
They regulate temperature better than adults.
Low temperature improves feeding.
Cold stress is harmless if the baby is sleeping.

questions.rationale: Hypothermia can contribute to hypoglycaemia and respiratory compromise.

questions.stem: Which intervention best supports newborn warmth?

options.text: Immediate bathing.
Drying promptly, skin-to-skin contact, warm clothing and a suitable environment.
Leaving the baby uncovered for observation.
Using cold surfaces for weighing.

questions.rationale: These measures reduce heat loss and support adaptation.

questions.stem: A newborn develops jaundice within the first 24 hours. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Treat it as a normal finding.
Increase feeding and wait several days.
Arrange prompt neonatal review.
Expose the baby to direct sunlight without assessment.

questions.rationale: Jaundice in the first day is a warning sign and requires evaluation.

questions.stem: Which assessment best evaluates feeding effectiveness?

options.text: Length of feeding only.
Maternal intention only.
Number of visitors.
Readiness, attachment, sucking, swallowing, output and weight trend.

questions.rationale: Effective feeding requires observation of technique and evidence of intake.

questions.stem: A newborn has persistent low temperature despite warming measures. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Escalate for review and assess for hypoglycaemia, infection or other causes.
Continue routine care only.
Assume the room is cold.
Delay feeding indefinitely.

questions.rationale: Persistent hypothermia may indicate illness and requires investigation.

questions.stem: Which finding is most concerning in a newborn?

options.text: Occasional sneezing.
Poor feeding with lethargy and temperature instability.
Brief hiccups.
Sleeping between feeds.

questions.rationale: The combination may indicate systemic illness.

questions.stem: Why should identification checks be completed carefully for newborns?

options.text: They are only administrative.
They are unnecessary if the mother recognises the baby.
To prevent wrong-baby and wrong-mother errors during care and transfer.
They are needed only before discharge.

questions.rationale: Reliable identification protects mother and baby throughout care.

questions.stem: A newborn has a seizure-like episode. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Restrain the limbs.
Feed the baby immediately.
Wait to see if it happens again.
Protect airway and safety, observe and time the event, and obtain urgent neonatal assistance.

questions.rationale: Seizures are a neonatal emergency requiring immediate assessment.

questions.stem: Which family teaching is most important before newborn discharge?

options.text: Signs such as poor feeding, breathing difficulty, fever or low temperature, increasing jaundice, lethargy or seizures require urgent help.
The baby should sleep through the night immediately.
All crying indicates hunger.
Jaundice is always normal.

questions.rationale: Families need clear warning signs and escalation advice.

questions.stem: A newborn is cold and has low blood glucose. How are these findings related?

options.text: Hypothermia always raises blood glucose.
Cold stress increases glucose use and can contribute to hypoglycaemia.
The findings are unrelated.
Low glucose improves temperature control.

questions.rationale: Newborns use glucose to generate heat, increasing hypoglycaemia risk during cold stress.

questions.stem: Which action best supports bonding and feeding?

options.text: Routine separation.
Delaying contact until after bathing.
Early skin-to-skin contact when clinically safe.
Restricting parental involvement.

questions.rationale: Skin-to-skin contact supports warmth, bonding and feeding readiness.

questions.stem: A newborn has poor colour but is breathing normally. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ignore colour if breathing is present.
Feed immediately.
Wait until the Apgar score is complete.
Assess circulation, oxygenation and overall adaptation rather than assuming the baby is stable.

questions.rationale: Colour is part of immediate adaptation and requires assessment in context.

questions.stem: Why should cord care follow local policy?

options.text: To reduce infection risk and ensure consistent safe practice.
Cord care has no safety implications.
Any household product is acceptable.
The cord should always be covered tightly.

questions.rationale: Safe cord care reduces contamination and infection risk.

questions.stem: A mother says the baby is too sleepy to feed and has had few wet nappies. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure her without assessment.
Assess feeding, hydration, weight, temperature and clinical condition, and escalate if concerning.
Advise waiting 24 hours.
Recommend water supplementation.

questions.rationale: Poor feeding and low output may indicate inadequate intake or illness.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes normal transition from danger signs?

options.text: Any sleepiness is normal.
Any crying is abnormal.
Brief adaptation changes may resolve, but persistent respiratory distress, poor feeding, lethargy or temperature instability require review.
A normal Apgar score excludes later problems.

questions.rationale: Persistence, severity and associated findings help distinguish normal adaptation from illness.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe newborn nursing care?

options.text: The baby is discharged quickly.
Only weight is monitored.
Apgar scoring is completed once.
The baby is kept warm, assessed systematically, supported to feed and monitored for warning signs while the family receives clear education.

questions.rationale: Safe newborn care combines adaptation assessment, thermoregulation, feeding support, ongoing monitoring and family education.

questions.stem: A woman at 35 weeks presents with severe epigastric pain, visual disturbance and a markedly elevated blood pressure. Fetal movement is present but reduced. Which nursing response is the highest priority?

options.text: Initiate urgent escalation for severe preeclampsia, prepare prescribed treatment and closely monitor maternal and fetal status.
Reassure her that upper abdominal discomfort is common late in pregnancy.
Advise rest in a dark room and repeat the blood pressure in two hours.
Arrange routine antenatal follow-up within the week.

questions.rationale: The combination of severe hypertension, visual disturbance and upper abdominal pain suggests severe preeclampsia with risk of seizure, stroke and organ dysfunction. Immediate structured escalation and close maternal-fetal monitoring are required.

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks has painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. Her observations are stable and fetal heart activity is present. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation.
Treat the episode as possible placenta previa, avoid unsafe vaginal examination until placental location is known and arrange urgent obstetric review.
Encourage ambulation to determine whether bleeding increases.
Discharge her if the bleeding slows.

questions.rationale: Painless bleeding may indicate placenta previa. Vaginal examination can worsen haemorrhage and should be avoided until placental location is confirmed.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks reports painful vaginal bleeding and a tender, rigid uterus. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Placenta previa.
Normal Braxton Hicks contractions.
Placental abruption.
Urinary tract infection.

questions.rationale: Painful bleeding with uterine tenderness is characteristic of placental abruption and requires urgent assessment.

questions.stem: A woman with gestational diabetes has several elevated blood glucose readings despite following her meal plan. What is the best nursing action?

options.text: Tell her that mild hyperglycaemia is expected in pregnancy.
Advise her to stop all carbohydrates.
Delay review until labour begins.
Review glucose trends, medication or insulin plan, nutrition and fetal surveillance needs with the multidisciplinary team.

questions.rationale: Persistent hyperglycaemia requires coordinated review because it can affect maternal and fetal outcomes.

questions.stem: A woman at 31 weeks reports regular painful contractions and pelvic pressure. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess for preterm labour, including contractions, cervical change, fluid loss and fetal wellbeing, and escalate promptly.
Advise rest at home and reassess the following day.
Explain that contractions before term are always Braxton Hicks.
Encourage walking to see whether contractions become stronger.

questions.rationale: Regular contractions and pelvic pressure before term may indicate preterm labour and need prompt evaluation.

questions.stem: A high-risk pregnant woman has a rising blood pressure trend but no headache or visual symptoms. How should the nurse respond?

options.text: Ignore the trend because severe symptoms are absent.
Recognise that worsening trends may precede symptoms, repeat assessment, review urine and laboratory findings and escalate as indicated.
Wait for the next scheduled visit.
Ask the woman to self-monitor only.

questions.rationale: Hypertensive disorders may progress before severe symptoms appear. Trends and associated findings must be assessed.

questions.stem: Which finding in a woman with preeclampsia most strongly suggests worsening disease?

options.text: Mild ankle swelling after standing.
Occasional heartburn.
New right upper abdominal pain and abnormal liver tests.
Urinary frequency.

questions.rationale: Upper abdominal pain and abnormal liver results may indicate severe organ involvement.

questions.stem: A woman with suspected placenta previa asks why the nurse will not perform a vaginal examination. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The examination is unnecessary in all pregnant women.
The examination is only performed after birth.
The examination would not provide useful information.
If the placenta is covering the cervix, examination could provoke severe bleeding, so placental location must be confirmed first.

questions.rationale: The explanation supports informed care and reflects the risk of haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks says her baby's movements have reduced over the past day. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Perform prompt fetal assessment and escalate reduced movement according to local policy.
Reassure her because fetal movement normally decreases near term.
Advise her to wait until the next morning.
Recommend increased physical activity.

questions.rationale: Reduced fetal movement may indicate fetal compromise and requires timely assessment.

questions.stem: Which information is most important in an ISBAR escalation for a woman with severe preeclampsia?

options.text: Only the diagnosis.
Current blood pressure, symptoms, relevant laboratory findings, fetal status and the urgent action required.
The woman's full social history.
A general statement that she looks unwell.

questions.rationale: Structured escalation should communicate the clinical situation, evidence of severity and a clear recommendation.

questions.stem: A woman with gestational diabetes becomes sweaty, shaky and confused after insulin. What is the priority?

options.text: Encourage exercise.
Give the next insulin dose.
Check blood glucose immediately and treat suspected hypoglycaemia according to protocol.
Wait for the symptoms to settle.

questions.rationale: The symptoms suggest hypoglycaemia, which requires immediate assessment and treatment.

questions.stem: A woman at 29 weeks reports leaking fluid but no contractions. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume urinary leakage.
Advise her to use a pad and wait two days.
Recommend pelvic floor exercises only.
Arrange prompt assessment for possible preterm rupture of membranes and evaluate maternal and fetal wellbeing.

questions.rationale: Leaking fluid before term may indicate membrane rupture and carries infection and preterm-birth risks.

questions.stem: Which assessment best reflects integrated care in a high-risk pregnancy?

options.text: Maternal observations, symptoms, laboratory trends, fetal growth, fetal movement and fetal heart assessment.
Maternal blood pressure alone.
Fetal heart rate alone.
Ultrasound results only.

questions.rationale: High-risk assessment must integrate maternal and fetal information.

questions.stem: A woman with hypertension in pregnancy asks why laboratory tests are repeated. Which explanation is best?

options.text: They are repeated only to confirm the diagnosis.
They help identify organ involvement and worsening disease before symptoms become severe.
They replace blood pressure monitoring.
They are routine and have no clinical significance.

questions.rationale: Laboratory trends may show renal, hepatic, haematological or other organ dysfunction.

questions.stem: A woman with a high-risk pregnancy declines a recommended test because of fear. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed without further discussion.
Ask the family to overrule her.
Explore her concerns, explain benefits, risks and alternatives, support informed choice and communicate the decision to the team.
Document refusal and end the conversation.

questions.rationale: Shared decision-making requires respectful explanation and exploration of concerns.

questions.stem: A woman with suspected placental abruption is becoming pale and tachycardic, but visible bleeding is limited. What should the nurse consider?

options.text: The blood loss is minor because little is visible.
The tachycardia is due to anxiety only.
The condition is stable if fetal movement is present.
Concealed haemorrhage may be occurring and urgent escalation is required.

questions.rationale: Placental abruption may involve concealed bleeding and significant maternal compromise.

questions.stem: Which nursing action best supports a woman with gestational diabetes before discharge?

options.text: Use teach-back to confirm glucose monitoring, medication use, warning signs and follow-up plans.
Provide a generic diet leaflet only.
Ask her family to manage the condition.
Avoid discussing possible complications.

questions.rationale: Teach-back confirms practical understanding and supports safe self-management.

questions.stem: A woman at 33 weeks has fever, uterine tenderness and reduced fetal movement. What is the best response?

options.text: Provide routine advice and reassess later.
Assess for infection and fetal compromise and arrange urgent review.
Encourage oral fluids only.
Assume normal pregnancy discomfort.

questions.rationale: Infection with fetal change is potentially serious and requires urgent assessment.

questions.stem: Why should mother and fetus be monitored together in high-risk pregnancy?

options.text: Fetal assessment is unnecessary if the mother feels well.
Maternal observations are enough to predict fetal status.
Maternal and fetal conditions can affect each other and deterioration may occur in either.
The two assessments are unrelated.

questions.rationale: High-risk maternity care requires simultaneous consideration of maternal and fetal wellbeing.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe high-risk pregnancy care?

options.text: All appointments are completed.
The woman receives written information only.
Care is based on one isolated observation.
Abnormal trends are identified early, communicated clearly and managed through coordinated maternal-fetal assessment.

questions.rationale: Safe care depends on early recognition, structured escalation, monitoring and shared decision-making.

questions.stem: Immediately after rupture of membranes, the fetal heart rate falls sharply and the umbilical cord is visible at the vaginal opening. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Call for emergency assistance, relieve pressure on the cord according to protocol, position the woman and prepare for urgent birth.
Wait for the obstetrician before touching the woman.
Encourage the woman to push.
Cover the cord and continue routine monitoring.

questions.rationale: Cord prolapse threatens fetal oxygenation and requires immediate pressure relief and urgent birth preparation.

questions.stem: A woman develops heavy bleeding shortly after birth, a boggy uterus, tachycardia and falling blood pressure. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Observe for 15 minutes to confirm the trend.
Activate the postpartum haemorrhage response, assess and massage the uterus where appropriate, support prescribed medication and fluids and prepare for blood products.
Encourage oral fluids.
Transfer her to the postnatal ward for monitoring.

questions.rationale: This is a time-critical postpartum haemorrhage requiring coordinated emergency management.

questions.stem: During birth, the baby's head delivers but the shoulders do not. What should the nurse recognise?

options.text: Normal slow progress.
Placenta previa.
Shoulder dystocia requiring immediate team activation and established manoeuvres.
Cord prolapse.

questions.rationale: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency requiring prompt coordinated response.

questions.stem: A labouring woman with a previous uterine scar develops sudden severe abdominal pain, fetal bradycardia and loss of fetal station. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Normal transition.
Postpartum haemorrhage.
Gestational diabetes.
Uterine rupture.

questions.rationale: These findings are classic warning signs of uterine rupture and require immediate surgical response.

questions.stem: A woman suddenly becomes hypoxic, hypotensive and collapses during labour. What is the nursing priority?

options.text: Begin resuscitation, activate emergency obstetric and critical-care support and coordinate rapidly.
Complete a detailed history.
Wait for diagnostic confirmation.
Move the woman to a quiet room.

questions.rationale: Sudden collapse may indicate amniotic fluid embolism or another catastrophic event and requires immediate resuscitation.

questions.stem: Why is role clarity important during an obstetric emergency?

options.text: It allows one person to perform all tasks.
It reduces duplication, delay and omitted actions during a rapidly changing event.
It removes the need for communication.
It is needed only after the emergency.

questions.rationale: Clear roles support coordinated and timely care.

questions.stem: Which communication method is most appropriate during emergency medication administration?

options.text: Unconfirmed verbal instructions.
Non-verbal gestures only.
Closed-loop communication with read-back and confirmation.
Documentation after the event without verbal communication.

questions.rationale: Closed-loop communication reduces error under pressure.

questions.stem: A woman with postpartum haemorrhage remains hypotensive after initial treatment. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the treatment will work later.
Stop monitoring.
Encourage ambulation.
Continue urgent reassessment and escalate for ongoing haemorrhage and advanced management.

questions.rationale: Persistent hypotension suggests ongoing blood loss or inadequate response.

questions.stem: During cord prolapse management, what is the main physiological goal?

options.text: Reduce pressure on the cord to protect fetal oxygenation until birth.
Increase uterine contractions.
Delay birth.
Promote maternal ambulation.

questions.rationale: Compression of the cord compromises fetal blood flow and oxygenation.

questions.stem: A woman experiencing an emergency birth becomes visibly frightened. What should the nurse do while emergency care continues?

options.text: Avoid communication to prevent distraction.
Use brief, clear explanations, reassurance and involve her chosen support person where possible.
Promise that everything will be fine.
Ask the family to explain the situation.

questions.rationale: Urgency does not remove the need for respectful, compassionate communication.

questions.stem: Which finding is most concerning after treatment begins for postpartum haemorrhage?

options.text: Bleeding slows and blood pressure improves.
The uterus becomes firm.
The woman becomes more confused and urine output falls.
The pulse rate decreases.

questions.rationale: Confusion and oliguria suggest worsening hypoperfusion.

questions.stem: A woman with suspected uterine rupture is being prepared for emergency surgery. What should the nurse prioritise?

options.text: Complete routine discharge documentation.
Delay transfer until all notes are finalised.
Encourage oral intake.
Continue maternal and fetal monitoring, support resuscitation and provide concise handover.

questions.rationale: Transfer should occur with ongoing stabilisation, monitoring and clear communication.

questions.stem: A shoulder dystocia emergency has resolved. What should happen after birth?

options.text: Assess mother and newborn for complications, document events and participate in debriefing.
No further action is required.
Discuss the event only if injury occurred.
Avoid family communication.

questions.rationale: Post-event assessment and learning are important because maternal and neonatal complications may follow.

questions.stem: Which action should be avoided in cord prolapse?

options.text: Calling for emergency assistance.
Allowing pressure to remain on the cord while waiting passively.
Positioning the woman to reduce compression.
Preparing for urgent birth.

questions.rationale: Passive delay risks prolonged fetal hypoxia.

questions.stem: A woman with massive postpartum haemorrhage requires blood products. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Delay until haemoglobin results are repeated.
Ask the family to consent for each unit if the woman is conscious.
Prepare and administer according to emergency protocol with required checks and ongoing monitoring.
Stop all other monitoring.

questions.rationale: Blood-product support is time-critical and requires safe verification and monitoring.

questions.stem: What is the best reason to use established emergency protocols?

options.text: They remove the need for judgement.
They apply only to junior staff.
They prevent all adverse outcomes.
They provide a reliable sequence of critical actions during high-stress events.

questions.rationale: Protocols support timely coordinated response while clinical judgement remains essential.

questions.stem: A patient collapses and the cause is uncertain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Respond to airway, breathing and circulation threats immediately while activating the emergency team.
Wait for a diagnosis.
Complete documentation first.
Ask the family for a full history before intervening.

questions.rationale: Resuscitation priorities should not wait for diagnostic certainty.

questions.stem: Which handover is best during transfer after an obstetric emergency?

options.text: A task list only.
A concise summary of the event, maternal and fetal or newborn status, interventions, response, risks and outstanding actions.
The woman's full antenatal history only.
A verbal statement that she is unstable.

questions.rationale: Risk-focused handover supports continuity and safe transfer.

questions.stem: Why is emotional support still important during an obstetric emergency?

options.text: It delays treatment.
It is only needed after recovery.
It supports dignity, trust and participation during a frightening event.
It replaces clinical intervention.

questions.rationale: Compassionate communication remains part of safe care.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective emergency maternity nursing?

options.text: The event is managed by one person.
Documentation is completed before treatment.
The family is excluded.
Help is activated early, protocols are followed, maternal-fetal oxygenation is protected and communication remains clear.

questions.rationale: Effective emergency response combines rapid action, teamwork, monitoring and communication.

questions.stem: A premature newborn develops grunting, chest retractions and falling oxygen saturation. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Maintain warmth, support airway and breathing, apply prescribed respiratory support and urgently involve the neonatal team.
Wait to see whether the baby settles.
Feed the baby immediately.
Move the baby away from monitors to reduce stimulation.

questions.rationale: These are signs of respiratory distress and require immediate assessment and neonatal support.

questions.stem: Why are premature newborns especially vulnerable to hypothermia?

options.text: They generate more heat than term newborns.
They have limited fat stores and lose heat quickly.
They regulate temperature independently.
Hypothermia is uncommon in prematurity.

questions.rationale: Premature infants have limited thermoregulatory capacity.

questions.stem: A growth-restricted newborn is jittery and feeding poorly. What should the nurse consider?

options.text: Normal adaptation only.
Excessive feeding.
Possible hypoglycaemia requiring prompt glucose assessment.
Post-term maturity.

questions.rationale: Growth-restricted newborns are at risk of unstable blood glucose.

questions.stem: A newborn has central cyanosis and episodes of apnoea. What is the priority?

options.text: Routine skin-to-skin care only.
Delay assessment until the next feed.
Provide oral glucose first.
Urgent airway and breathing support and neonatal escalation.

questions.rationale: Central cyanosis and apnoea indicate severe respiratory compromise.

questions.stem: Which combination may indicate neonatal sepsis?

options.text: Temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy and respiratory change.
Occasional sneezing and hiccups.
Brief crying before feeds.
Sleeping between feeds.

questions.rationale: Neonatal sepsis can present subtly and deteriorate quickly.

questions.stem: A high-risk newborn has jaundice that is worsening. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume all jaundice is normal.
Assess severity and timing, review bilirubin monitoring and escalate for treatment according to policy.
Expose the baby to direct sunlight only.
Delay review until discharge.

questions.rationale: Worsening jaundice requires evaluation and may need phototherapy or other treatment.

questions.stem: Which assessment best evaluates a high-risk newborn?

options.text: Weight only.
Apgar score only.
Breathing, colour, tone, temperature, feeding, glucose risk, output and behavioural changes.
Maternal history only.

questions.rationale: Systematic ongoing assessment is essential because deterioration may be subtle.

questions.stem: A premature newborn tires during feeding and oxygen saturation falls. What is the best response?

options.text: Continue feeding to complete the volume.
Increase flow without assessment.
Feed more quickly.
Stop or pause the feed, assess breathing and coordination and seek neonatal guidance.

questions.rationale: Feeding intolerance with desaturation suggests instability and aspiration risk.

questions.stem: Why should subtle changes in a high-risk newborn be taken seriously?

options.text: Newborns may deteriorate rapidly and early signs can be non-specific.
Only severe symptoms are significant.
Premature babies normally appear unwell.
Monitoring causes unnecessary concern.

questions.rationale: Early recognition is critical in vulnerable newborns.

questions.stem: Which action best supports thermoregulation in a premature newborn?

options.text: Bathe immediately.
Use a controlled warm environment and minimise unnecessary heat loss while monitoring temperature.
Leave uncovered for observation.
Use cold weighing surfaces.

questions.rationale: Premature infants need active thermoregulation support.

questions.stem: A newborn with suspected sepsis becomes mottled and less responsive. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait for culture results.
Offer another feed.
Escalate urgently and support stabilisation while treatment is prepared.
Reduce monitoring to allow rest.

questions.rationale: Mottling and reduced responsiveness suggest worsening perfusion and severe illness.

questions.stem: A high-risk newborn is receiving oxygen. Which assessment is essential?

options.text: Temperature only.
Feeding volume only.
Parental anxiety only.
Oxygen saturation, respiratory effort, colour and response to therapy.

questions.rationale: Oxygen therapy requires close monitoring of respiratory status and effectiveness.

questions.stem: Why are low-birth-weight newborns at risk of hypoglycaemia?

options.text: They may have limited energy stores and increased metabolic needs.
They always receive too much milk.
They cannot absorb glucose.
Hypoglycaemia is unrelated to birth weight.

questions.rationale: Limited glycogen and fat stores increase risk.

questions.stem: A newborn receiving phototherapy becomes less interested in feeding. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ignore feeding while phototherapy continues.
Assess hydration, feeding effectiveness and overall condition and escalate concerns.
Stop phototherapy independently.
Provide water only.

questions.rationale: Treatment does not remove the need for ongoing feeding and clinical assessment.

questions.stem: Which parental communication is most appropriate when a newborn requires escalation?

options.text: Avoid all discussion until the baby improves.
Provide only technical terminology.
Use calm, clear language about what is happening and involve parents where clinically possible.
Ask another family member to explain.

questions.rationale: Clear compassionate communication supports family-centred care.

questions.stem: A newborn has a low temperature and low blood glucose. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The findings are unrelated.
Low glucose improves temperature control.
Hypothermia reduces metabolic needs.
Cold stress may increase glucose use and worsen hypoglycaemia.

questions.rationale: Thermoregulation and glucose stability are closely linked.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests respiratory distress rather than normal transition?

options.text: Persistent grunting with retractions and central cyanosis.
Brief irregular breathing without colour change.
Occasional sneezing.
Transient hiccups.

questions.rationale: Persistent work of breathing and cyanosis are danger signs.

questions.stem: A parent asks why the newborn is monitored so frequently. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Monitoring is mainly for documentation.
High-risk newborns can change quickly, and frequent assessment helps identify early deterioration.
All newborns require identical intensive monitoring.
The equipment replaces nursing assessment.

questions.rationale: Frequent assessment is justified by vulnerability and rapid change.

questions.stem: A premature newborn has poor feeding, lethargy and temperature instability but no fever. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Rule out infection.
Wait for a rash.
Assess for neonatal sepsis and escalate despite the absence of fever.
Continue routine care.

questions.rationale: Neonatal infection may present without fever and with subtle signs.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe high-risk newborn care?

options.text: Only weight gain is monitored.
Parents are excluded from care.
Apgar scoring is used as the sole assessment.
Respiratory distress, glucose instability and infection signs are recognised early while warmth, feeding and family communication are maintained.

questions.rationale: Safe care combines close assessment, stabilisation and family-centred communication.

questions.stem: A woman with limited English requires an urgent caesarean birth. Which nursing action best supports culturally safe care?

options.text: Arrange a professional interpreter, explain the situation in clear steps, check understanding and involve her chosen support person where possible.
Use a family member as interpreter for all consent discussions.
Proceed without explanation because the situation is urgent.
Ask staff to communicate only after surgery.

questions.rationale: Urgency does not remove the need for accessible, respectful communication and informed participation.

questions.stem: What is the best way to identify a woman's cultural preferences?

options.text: Assume preferences based on her background.
Ask respectfully what matters to her and her family.
Use a standard cultural checklist only.
Ask another patient from the same community.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety requires asking rather than stereotyping.

questions.stem: A woman declines a recommended intervention after receiving information. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Coerce her because the recommendation is evidence based.
Ask the family to overrule her.
Confirm understanding, explore concerns, respect the informed decision and communicate it to the team.
Document refusal and avoid further discussion.

questions.rationale: Consent is ongoing and informed refusal should be respected within legal and safety requirements.

questions.stem: Which situation most clearly requires a professional interpreter?

options.text: A routine greeting.
Offering water.
Explaining visiting hours.
A complex discussion about emergency birth, risks and consent.

questions.rationale: High-risk or complex information requires accurate professional interpretation.

questions.stem: A woman has a history of traumatic birth and becomes distressed during an examination. What is the most appropriate nursing response?

options.text: Pause if safe, explain each step, seek consent, offer choices and use a trauma-informed approach.
Continue quickly to finish the procedure.
Ask her partner to restrain her.
Avoid acknowledging the distress.

questions.rationale: Trauma-informed care promotes safety, control and dignity.

questions.stem: A family's cultural practice is important to them and does not create clinical risk. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Prohibit it because it is unfamiliar.
Accommodate the practice where possible.
Ignore the request.
Ask the family to leave.

questions.rationale: Safe cultural practices should be respected and incorporated.

questions.stem: A woman with hearing impairment needs discharge education. What is the best approach?

options.text: Speak more loudly from behind her.
Give written information only.
Use accessible communication methods, visual material and teach-back.
Ask the family to interpret all content.

questions.rationale: Communication should be adapted to individual needs and understanding confirmed.

questions.stem: What does informed choice require?

options.text: A signed form only.
Agreement with the clinician.
Family approval in every case.
Clear information about options, benefits, risks and alternatives with time for questions.

questions.rationale: Informed choice depends on understanding and voluntary participation.

questions.stem: A woman experiences pregnancy loss. Which response is most compassionate?

options.text: Offer privacy, clear compassionate communication, memory-making where appropriate and referral to support services.
Avoid discussing the baby.
Encourage rapid discharge without support.
Use routine language to minimise emotion.

questions.rationale: Bereavement care should acknowledge loss and provide individualised support.

questions.stem: A support person asks to remain during an urgent procedure, and the woman wants them present. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Exclude them automatically.
Include the support person where clinically and safely possible.
Ask the support person to make decisions.
Delay treatment until they leave.

questions.rationale: Family involvement should reflect the woman's wishes and clinical safety.

questions.stem: Which action best supports shared decision-making during high-risk maternity care?

options.text: Provide one recommendation only.
Use technical language to ensure accuracy.
Present options and likely outcomes, explore preferences and agree on a plan where possible.
Avoid discussing uncertainty.

questions.rationale: Shared decision-making combines evidence with informed patient preferences.

questions.stem: A woman has low health literacy and is being discharged with a complex newborn feeding plan. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Provide a detailed technical leaflet only.
Ask her to search online.
Reduce the plan without consulting the team.
Use plain language, demonstration, a simple written plan and teach-back.

questions.rationale: Accessible education and teach-back improve safety.

questions.stem: A family member insists on receiving confidential information, but the woman has not consented. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Respect confidentiality and clarify whom the woman wants involved.
Provide the information because they are family.
Discuss it outside the room.
Ask another nurse to decide.

questions.rationale: Family-centred care does not override confidentiality.

questions.stem: A woman expresses a spiritual preference that conflicts with a non-negotiable emergency requirement. What is the best response?

options.text: Ignore the preference.
Explain the safety requirement respectfully and explore acceptable alternatives.
Allow unsafe care.
Ask the family to decide.

questions.rationale: Respect should be balanced with evidence-based safety.

questions.stem: Why is consent described as an ongoing process?

options.text: Because signatures expire every hour.
Because only doctors can confirm consent.
Because understanding and willingness may change as the situation and options change.
Because emergencies remove consent requirements.

questions.rationale: Patients should remain informed and involved as care evolves.

questions.stem: Which communication approach is most appropriate after an emergency neonatal transfer?

options.text: Promise a positive outcome.
Avoid the family until the diagnosis is confirmed.
Use only technical terms.
Provide honest updates, acknowledge uncertainty and explain the next steps.

questions.rationale: Clear and compassionate communication supports families during uncertainty.

questions.stem: A woman says staff are making assumptions about her feeding choices. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explore her goals and preferences without judgement and provide balanced information.
Tell her the standard approach must be followed.
Ask her family to choose.
Avoid discussing feeding.

questions.rationale: Cultural and family-centred care requires individualised, non-judgemental discussion.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates trauma-informed maternity care?

options.text: All procedures are completed quickly.
The woman is informed, offered choices, treated respectfully and supported to retain control where possible.
Distress is ignored to avoid delay.
The family makes all decisions.

questions.rationale: Trauma-informed care emphasises safety, choice, collaboration and dignity.

questions.stem: A bereaved family requests time and privacy with their baby. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Refuse because the baby has died.
Limit contact to a few minutes without discussion.
Support the request where clinically and legally appropriate and offer further resources.
Avoid memory-making options.

questions.rationale: Compassionate bereavement care should be individualised and respectful.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects culturally safe, family-centred maternity care?

options.text: Everyone receives identical care.
Families make all decisions.
Urgent care is delivered without explanation.
Care is clinically safe while communication, informed choice, cultural preferences and compassionate support are maintained.

questions.rationale: Safe care integrates evidence, respect, access and participation.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: A maternity service finds that women from one cultural community report feeling ignored during labour and are less likely to ask questions. Which leadership response best reflects respectful maternity care?

options.text: Meet with women and community representatives, examine care experiences and redesign communication and consent practices with measurable standards.
Provide staff with a reminder to be polite.
Ask families to raise concerns after discharge.
Use the same communication approach for all women to avoid differences.

questions.rationale: Respectful maternity care requires dignity, informed choice and freedom from discrimination. Leaders should use patient experience data and co-design practical improvements rather than rely on reminders alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: Junior staff hesitate to activate an obstetric emergency call because they fear criticism if the situation proves less serious than expected. What should the nurse leader do?

options.text: Require medical approval before any activation.
Clarify escalation criteria, reinforce that clinical concern is a valid trigger, use simulation and provide supportive debriefing.
Reduce the number of emergency drills.
Ask junior nurses to escalate only through senior midwives.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety supports early escalation. Clear criteria, simulation and non-punitive debriefing help staff act promptly while preserving accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: Which activity best demonstrates clinical governance in maternity services?

options.text: Informal discussion among experienced staff.
Reliance on individual clinical judgement only.
Policies, credentialing, audit, incident review and outcome monitoring linked to leadership action.
Annual education without monitoring.

questions.rationale: Clinical governance provides structured oversight through policy, competence assurance, audit, review and monitoring.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: A unit performs regular emergency drills, but response times remain inconsistent. What should leaders examine next?

options.text: Whether staff enjoyed the simulation.
Only the number of staff who attended.
Whether the drill scenario was realistic enough.
Role clarity, equipment availability, workflow and whether learning is transferred into real practice.

questions.rationale: Simulation is useful only when system factors and translation into practice are evaluated.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: A woman reports feeling coerced into a procedure during labour. What is the most appropriate leadership response?

options.text: Review the incident respectfully, examine consent and communication processes, support the woman and address system and staff learning.
Explain that emergency care sometimes requires rapid decisions.
Assume the procedure was justified and take no action.
Refer the issue only to legal services.

questions.rationale: Respectful care includes informed choice and freedom from mistreatment. Leaders should review both the individual experience and the system conditions that enabled it.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates psychological safety within a maternity team?

options.text: Emergency calls decrease to near zero.
Staff ask questions, admit uncertainty and escalate abnormal findings without humiliation.
Only senior clinicians raise concerns.
Near misses are discussed informally but not reported.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety is demonstrated when staff can speak up early and safely.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: A new graduate is assigned to manage a high-risk labour without adequate supervision. Which leadership principle has been breached?

options.text: Respectful care only.
Confidentiality.
Alignment of staff competence and support with patient acuity.
Patient education.

questions.rationale: Safe services require that competence, staffing and supervision match clinical risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: Which approach best strengthens emergency readiness for postpartum haemorrhage?

options.text: A single annual lecture.
Posting the protocol on the wall.
Relying on experienced staff to lead without drills.
Regular multidisciplinary simulation, standardised equipment, role allocation and post-event review.

questions.rationale: Readiness depends on capability, equipment, role clarity and repeated practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: A leader notices that respectful care standards deteriorate during high workload. What is the best action?

options.text: Review staffing, workflow and priorities so dignity, consent and communication remain reliable.
Accept reduced communication during busy periods.
Tell women to be patient.
Reduce documentation of patient experience.

questions.rationale: Respectful care is a safety standard and should not disappear under pressure.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: Which measure would best evaluate respectful maternity care?

options.text: Number of policies issued.
Patient-reported experience of dignity, communication and involvement, reviewed across different groups.
Average length of stay.
Number of staff meetings.

questions.rationale: Respectful care should be measured through patient experience and equity data.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: A senior clinician publicly dismisses a junior nurse's concern about fetal deterioration. What should the service leader do?

options.text: Ignore the interaction because the senior clinician is accountable.
Ask the junior nurse to be more confident next time.
Address the behaviour, reinforce escalation expectations and ensure the patient is reviewed.
Delay action until the annual performance review.

questions.rationale: Hierarchy and humiliation undermine psychological safety and can delay care.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects fair accountability?

options.text: Every incident should receive the same response.
Only system factors should be considered.
No accountability should follow self-reporting.
Leaders distinguish human error, at-risk behaviour and reckless behaviour while examining system contributors.

questions.rationale: Fair accountability balances learning with proportionate response to behaviour and context.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: A maternity service introduces a new fetal monitoring protocol. What is needed beyond policy publication?

options.text: Training, equipment, workflow integration, competency assessment and audit.
A staff email only.
Patient information only.
No further action if the guideline is evidence-based.

questions.rationale: Evidence-based policy must be translated into reliable practice through implementation supports.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: A woman with limited English is excluded from discussions because the team is busy. Which leadership standard is most relevant?

options.text: Efficiency.
Communication access and informed participation.
Documentation volume.
Staff autonomy.

questions.rationale: Respectful care requires communication access, including interpreter use where needed.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services
questions.stem: Which action best develops clinical judgement in maternity emergencies?
